questions.stem: What is a hydrocarbon?
options: A compound made of hydrogen, carbon and oxygen
A mixture of hydrogen gas and powdered carbon
A compound made of hydrogen and carbon atoms only
Any compound that contains at least one carbon atom
questions.explanation: Hydrocarbons, such as methane, propane and octane, contain only hydrogen and carbon atoms bonded together. Many carbon compounds contain other elements too, such as the oxygen in ethanol or glucose, so containing carbon is not enough. A hydrocarbon is a compound with chemical bonds, not a mixture of the two elements.

questions.stem: What is the general formula of the alkanes?
options: CnH2n
CnH2n−2
CnHn
CnH2n+2
questions.explanation: Every alkane fits CnH2n+2: methane is CH4 (n = 1), ethane C2H6 and propane C3H8. Each carbon has two hydrogens along the chain, plus one extra hydrogen at each end, which is where the +2 comes from. CnH2n fits the alkenes, such as ethene, C2H4, which have a double bond.

questions.stem: What is the name of the alkane C3H8?
options: Propane
Ethane
Butane
Pentane
questions.explanation: Alkane names show the number of carbon atoms: meth- 1, eth- 2, prop- 3, but- 4, pent- 5, hex- 6, hept- 7 and oct- 8, all ending in '-ane'. C3H8 has three carbons, so it is propane, the fuel in barbecue gas bottles. Butane, C4H10, is the fuel in cigarette lighters.

questions.stem: Which crude oil fraction is used as jet fuel for aircraft?
options: Refinery gas
Fuel oil
Kerosene
Bitumen
questions.explanation: Kerosene, with molecules of roughly 10 to 16 carbon atoms, is a liquid that burns cleanly and is used as jet fuel. Bitumen is the thick, sticky residue used to surface roads, and refinery gas, mostly propane and butane, is sold as bottled gas. Fuel oil is used in ships and some power stations.

questions.stem: How has the main use of crude oil changed since the mid-1800s?
options: From lamp oil, to transport fuels, to also making plastics
From plastics, to lamp oil, to transport fuels
From transport fuels, to lamp oil, to plastics
From road surfacing, to plastics, and then to lamp oil for lighting
questions.explanation: Early oil wells in the 1850s and 1860s were drilled mainly to make kerosene for lamps. Petrol and diesel engines then made transport fuels the main use in the 1900s, and from the mid-1900s oil also became the main raw material for plastics and many other chemicals. Plastics came last, so they cannot have been the first use.

questions.stem: What are the products when a hydrocarbon such as methane burns completely in plenty of oxygen?
options: Carbon monoxide and water
Carbon and hydrogen gas
Carbon dioxide and hydrogen
Carbon dioxide and water
questions.explanation: In complete combustion all the carbon becomes carbon dioxide and all the hydrogen becomes water: CH4 + 2O2 → CO2 + 2H2O. Carbon monoxide and soot form only when there is not enough oxygen, in incomplete combustion. Hydrogen does not escape as a gas, because it combines with oxygen.

questions.stem: What is a polymer?
options: A very long chain molecule made of many repeating monomers
A small molecule made of a few different elements
A mixture of many small molecules from crude oil
A material made by melting two or more metals together into one
questions.explanation: Polymers are made of thousands of small units, called monomers, joined in long chains; polyethylene, for example, is made from ethene monomers. Natural polymers include cellulose in wood and paper, starch and proteins. A material made by melting metals together is an alloy, not a polymer.

questions.stem: Polyethylene, the plastic in many bags and bottles, is made from ethene. Where does most of this ethene come from?
options: Limestone rock
Crude oil and natural gas
Starch from wheat and corn
Cellulose from trees
questions.explanation: Most ethene is made by breaking down hydrocarbons from crude oil and natural gas, which is why most plastics depend on fossil fuels. Starch and cellulose are natural polymers, and a small amount of plastic is made from plant sources such as sugarcane, but this is a small share. Limestone is calcium carbonate and is used for cement, not plastics.

questions.stem: Which of these is an organic compound?
options: Carbon dioxide, CO2
Calcium carbonate, CaCO3
Sodium chloride, NaCl
Methane, CH4
questions.explanation: Organic compounds are based on carbon chains or rings bonded to hydrogen, so methane is organic. Carbon dioxide and carbonates such as calcium carbonate contain carbon but are classed as inorganic because they are simple compounds without carbon–hydrogen bonds. Sodium chloride contains no carbon at all.

questions.stem: What is the formula of hexane, the alkane with six carbon atoms?
options: C6H14
C6H12
C6H6
C6H10
questions.explanation: Using CnH2n+2 with n = 6 gives 2 × 6 + 2 = 14 hydrogen atoms, so hexane is C6H14. C6H12 is what you get from forgetting the extra two hydrogens at the ends of the chain. Always check an alkane formula against the general formula.

questions.stem: In the structural formula of ethane, C2H6, which bonds are drawn?
options: Eight C–H bonds and one C–C bond
Six C–H bonds and one C–C bond
Six C–H bonds and two C–C bonds
Four C–H bonds and one C–C bond
questions.explanation: The two carbon atoms are joined by one single bond, and each carbon bonds to three hydrogens, giving six C–H bonds. Each carbon then has four bonds in total, as carbon always does. Drawing two C–C bonds would make a double bond, which ethane, an alkane, does not have.

questions.stem: In a fractionating column, where is bitumen collected, and why?
options: At the bottom, as its very long molecules have the highest boiling points
At the top, as its very long molecules are the lightest and rise furthest up
At the bottom, as its short molecules condense first as the vapour cools
In the middle, as it boils at about the same temperature as petrol
questions.explanation: The column is hottest at the bottom and coolest at the top. Bitumen has the longest molecules and the highest boiling point, so it does not even vaporise and is drawn off at the bottom, while small molecules such as refinery gas rise to the top. Long molecules are heavier, not lighter, and they have high boiling points.

questions.stem: A Bunsen burner with its air hole closed gives a yellow, sooty flame. What is happening?
options: Limited oxygen causes complete combustion, producing only water vapour
Limited oxygen causes incomplete combustion, producing soot and carbon monoxide
Extra oxygen causes faster combustion, producing a much hotter, brighter yellow flame
The gas burns completely, but the soot comes from the burner's metal
questions.explanation: Closing the air hole limits the oxygen, so the gas burns incompletely; glowing particles of soot (carbon) make the flame yellow, and carbon monoxide also forms. Opening the air hole lets in more oxygen, giving a hotter, blue flame from complete combustion. The yellow flame is cooler, not hotter, and releases less energy.

questions.stem: Why is a faulty gas heater in a poorly ventilated room dangerous?
options: It releases unburnt methane, which is poisonous in very small amounts
It produces so much water vapour that the air in the closed room becomes unsafe to breathe
It can burn with too little oxygen, releasing colourless, odourless carbon monoxide
It burns with too much oxygen, releasing poisonous carbon dioxide gas
questions.explanation: When a heater gets too little air, the gas burns incompletely and produces carbon monoxide, which cannot be seen or smelled and stops the blood carrying oxygen. That is why heaters need servicing and rooms need ventilation. Carbon dioxide forms in complete combustion and is not the main danger from a faulty heater.

questions.stem: Why does a polyethylene bag last for many years in landfill, while a paper bag breaks down much sooner?
options: Paper reacts with oxygen in the air, but plastic contains no carbon
Microorganisms can digest the cellulose in paper but not the chains in polyethylene
Paper is not a polymer, so it simply dissolves away in rainwater
Polyethylene is much denser than paper, so air and water can never get in to reach its chains
questions.explanation: Paper is made of cellulose, a natural polymer that bacteria and fungi have enzymes to break down, so it is biodegradable. Few microorganisms can break down the long hydrocarbon chains of polyethylene, so it persists for decades or longer. Both materials are polymers containing carbon; the difference is whether decomposers can digest them.

questions.stem: A café switches from plastic cups to paper cups to help the environment. Which is a real environmental cost of the paper cups?
options: Paper cups can only be made from rare and endangered tree species
Making them uses trees, water and energy, and many have a plastic lining
Paper cups take much longer to break down in soil than plastic cups ever do
Paper is made from crude oil, so it uses up the same resource
questions.explanation: Paper cups need wood, large amounts of water and energy to make, and most are lined with a thin layer of plastic so they do not leak, which makes them hard to recycle. Every alternative to crude-oil materials, including bioplastics, paper and bamboo, has its own environmental costs. Paper is made from wood pulp, not crude oil, and it breaks down faster than plastic.

questions.stem: Pentane is a liquid at room temperature, but propane is a gas. Why?
options: Propane is not an alkane, so it behaves differently from pentane
Pentane's longer molecules attract each other more strongly, raising its boiling point
Pentane's molecules contain stronger covalent bonds that must all break before the liquid boils
Propane's molecules are larger, so they move apart more easily when heated
questions.explanation: Longer alkane molecules have stronger attractions between them, so more energy is needed to separate them and the boiling point is higher. Pentane (five carbons) boils at about 36 °C, while propane (three carbons) boils at about −42 °C. Boiling separates whole molecules; it does not break the covalent bonds inside them.

questions.stem: Why does complete combustion of a fuel release more energy than incomplete combustion of the same fuel?
options: The soot formed in incomplete combustion stores the heat and only releases it once it cools
All the carbon is fully oxidised to carbon dioxide instead of being left as carbon monoxide or soot
Complete combustion uses less oxygen, so less of the fuel's energy is wasted heating up the surrounding air
Incomplete combustion produces more water, and the water absorbs much of the energy released
questions.explanation: In complete combustion every carbon atom ends up in carbon dioxide, so all the possible bonds to oxygen form and the most energy is released. In incomplete combustion some carbon stays as carbon monoxide or soot, which still holds energy that could have been released. Complete combustion uses more oxygen, not less.

questions.stem: Why can a thermoplastic such as polyethylene be melted and reshaped, while a thermoset, such as the plastic in a saucepan handle, cannot?
options: Thermoset chains are cross-linked by strong bonds that heating cannot undo
Thermoplastic chains are cross-linked, and the cross-links let them slide
Thermosets contain metal atoms, which raise their melting point greatly
Thermoplastics are natural polymers, while thermosets are synthetic
questions.explanation: In a thermoplastic the long chains are held together only by weak forces, so heating lets them slide past each other and the plastic softens and can be remoulded and recycled. In a thermoset, strong covalent cross-links join the chains into one rigid network, so it chars rather than melts. That heat resistance is why thermosets are used for saucepan handles and electrical fittings.

questions.stem: Persistent chemicals carried on microplastics can build up to higher concentrations in predators such as tuna than in the plankton at the base of their food chain. Why?
options: Plankton break the chemicals down completely before they are eaten
Each predator eats many contaminated prey, so the chemicals accumulate at each level
Tuna produce the chemicals themselves as their stomachs digest the microplastics they eat
Microplastics float, so only fish near the surface ever take them in
questions.explanation: These chemicals are not broken down or excreted easily, so they build up in an animal's tissues over its life, which is bioaccumulation. Each animal higher in the food chain eats many contaminated organisms, so concentrations rise at every level. Microplastics are found at all depths of the ocean, from the surface to the deep sea floor.
